prompt: What runs during the gaps between audio callbacks on a bare-metal MCU synth?

options.text: Nothing; the CPU sleeps until the next callback
options.explanation: It may idle if there is nothing to do, but the main loop runs whenever no interrupt is active.

options.text: The main (foreground) loop and any other lower-priority work, such as reading knobs, parsing MIDI and updating displays
options.explanation: Correct. The callback preempts the main loop; when it returns, the main loop resumes.
Bare-metal firmware has no OS scheduler; there is just the main loop and interrupts.

options.text: Another copy of the audio callback, in parallel
options.explanation: On a single-core MCU, one callback runs at a time, once per block.

workedExample:
```
main  ===   =====   ====
cb       ##      ##     ##
```

The DMA interrupt triggers the callback (##). Everything else (===) is the main loop: controls, MIDI, display, logging.

prompt: In the Teensy Audio Library source, the I2S DMA interrupt calls `update_all()`, which only sets a software interrupt pending; the software interrupt (priority 208, where 255 is lowest) runs all audio objects. Why structure it this way?

options.text: To keep the DMA interrupt very short, while the long DSP work runs at a lower priority that other urgent interrupts can preempt
options.explanation: Correct. Data-moving and other time-critical interrupts stay responsive; the heavy update runs at low priority but still preempts the main loop.

options.text: Because DMA interrupts cannot call functions
options.explanation: ISRs can call functions; this is a design choice about priorities, not a limitation.

options.text: So the audio update runs in the main loop
options.explanation: A software interrupt is still an interrupt: it preempts the main loop, which is essential for meeting deadlines.

options.text: To make the audio update run twice per block
options.explanation: It runs once per block; the indirection changes priority, not frequency.

workedExample:
Two goals conflict: DMA servicing must be prompt, and DSP takes a long time.

1. The DMA ISR does minimal work, then pends the software IRQ.
2. When it exits, the software IRQ runs (it outranks the main loop).
3. Interrupts with a higher priority (for example serial MIDI data) can still preempt the DSP.

The update still has to finish within the block period.
